title: A delivery check's behaviour is described only by its own failure message
context: By 2026-09-27 check-workflow.js held about thirty rules and had changed twenty times in ten days, nearly once per Change. Each rule's behaviour was written three times: in the code, in WORKFLOW.md, and as a list in the delivery-workflow Feature. In blueprint-contract-guardrails a rule written from the WORKFLOW prose contradicted the gate-branch-state check, and two review rounds passed before a browser read exposed it. Product-code checks, such as the architecture and error-copy tests, were left out at G2 because a decision record governs either the product or the delivery process, not both.
decision: What a delivery-process check enforces — a check in scripts/, a git hook, or a CI job over the workflow, the Blueprint or its documents — is stated once, in the message it prints when it fails, and in its test. WORKFLOW.md names the command a step runs, not the rules that command applies, and Feature pages do not list those checks. A check whose only purpose is to require or forbid wording in another document is removed rather than kept in step with it. Checks on the product's own code are outside this record.

alternatives.option: Keep the list in WORKFLOW.md and drop only the Feature's copy
alternatives.reason: It halves the copies but keeps the one that contradicted the code this time; the prose and the code would still drift apart silently.

alternatives.option: Generate the WORKFLOW list from the checks
alternatives.reason: A generator and its drift test are more machinery to guard a list nobody needs before running the command, whose failures already say what is wrong.

consequences: A reader of WORKFLOW.md learns what a gate checks by running it or reading its failure messages, not from the contract.
Adding a check means writing a failure message a reader can act on, since that message is its only description.
